newsitem.title: SUDAN: French and Chinese firms explore for gold in Sudan.
newsitem.headline: French and Chinese firms explore for gold in Sudan.

text.p: Chinese and French firms are exploring for gold in northern and southern Sudan, some of it in an area which is the focus of the country's war with rebels, industry sources said on Thursday.

Sudan accounts for only a tiny fraction of the world's gold output, but a Sudanese-French joint venture is expanding exploration in north-east Sudan after five years of successful production at the African country's only mine.

And the Sudanese-Chinese Gold Mining Co Ltd has completed exploration for gold in the area near Kurmuk, which is in the hands of rebels and what Sudan says are Ethiopian forces bent on toppling the Khartoum government.

A diplomat in Khartoum told Reuters in an interview on Thursday the Chinese partner in the venture, identified only as being from China's Guangxi autonomous region, had submitted a feasibility study to the government after completing exploration that started in December 1995.
"They are waiting for approval from the government and after that both sides will formally sign an agreement to start exploiting the gold," he said.
He did not have details but thought the minimum production potential for the Chinese company to consider the project feasible was at least four tonnes.
Officials at the company could not be reached for comment.
Sudan awarded a licence to another Chinese firm, Dong Ling, in November to explore for gold in the north-east Sholai area. The diplomat said work would start in February at the earliest.

Sudan also has alluvial gold deposits in the Nile river area near Damazin, where rebels say they are planning to advance to gain control of a strategic dam providing about 80 percent of Khartoum's power.
Aid and agricultural workers said they frequently see villagers panning for the metal.
But Sudan's only producing mine is in the north-east, where a Sudan-French joint venture, Ariab Mining Co Ltd, started exploring in September in a 12,000 square km zone.
Bruno Cabrol, deputy general manager of Ariab, told Reuters this week that the exploration was taking place to the north of Ariab's gold mine about 450 km north-east of Khartoum in the Red Sea state.
The parent company of one of Ariab's shareholders, Mine Ore SA, is also exploring in an area of about 58,000 square km located north-west of the Ariab area.

"We are confident in the success of this place. We succeed to establish a profitable relationship here," he said. The government owns about 56 percent of Ariab and the rest is held by CCI, a private consortium of French civil engineering companies and Mine Ore.
Cabrol said the mine had 28 tonnes of recoverable gold left. All of Sudan's gold is exported to a refinery in the UK, an industry source said.
Sudan has said that in 1997 gold will constitute a source of budget revenue for the first time, accounting for 2.4 percent.
"In the Pharaonic period they were mining gold in north-east Sudan. But they were looking for small, rich deposits. Now we have all the technology and can mine low grades," Cabrol said.
Ariab expects gold production will decline to 4,055 kg in 1997 from 4,560 kg in 1996 as the company mines lower grades. It started mining in Sudan at the end of 1991.
